title: Checkpoint: four questions that run through law and tax
summary: The law and tax phase reduces to four questions a developer must answer before signing anything: what binds, who pays when it goes wrong, who taxes the result, and who is advising whom. This lesson revisits the hardest idea behind each, from the lawyer's seat.
body:
Mr Shabazz, seven weeks of law and tax come down to four questions you ask before every signature: what binds, who pays when it goes wrong, who taxes the result, and who is advising whom. If you can answer all four in writing, you are ready to sign. If you cannot, you are not.

Recall

Q. What should an engagement letter with an adviser state?

A. Who the client is, the scope of the work and what is excluded, the facts and documents relied on, the fee basis and the timetable. Advice covers only what the adviser was asked to look at.

Q. What is the difference between tax avoidance and tax evasion?

A. Avoidance uses the words of a rule against its purpose with real, disclosed transactions and invites anti-avoidance rules. Evasion relies on concealment or falsehood and is a crime.

Q. What is the development spread?

A. The difference between yield on cost and the market cap rate. It is the margin that pays the developer for taking construction and lease-up risk.

Why this matters

Law and tax are often treated as the advisers' department, something you hand over and get back as a signed opinion. That is how developers lose money they thought they had made. The advisers answer questions; you decide which questions get asked, and you carry the result. A checkpoint is the place to make sure you can ask the four questions from memory, because in the meeting where they matter, there will be no notes and someone will be pressing you to sign today. Everything here is concept, not a jurisdictional conclusion; verify the law and tax that apply to any real decision against the primary source and with counsel.

Question one: what binds?

The hardest idea from weeks 19 and 20 is that obligations come from words and conduct, not from intention. A contract binds what its words say, interpreted against the law that governs it, in the forum that will hear disputes about it. A letter of intent binds what it says binds, and sometimes more if the parties behave as though they have a deal. Conditions decide when obligations start; promises decide what each party must do.

The applied test is a single sentence for each document: "This binds us to X, from the moment Y, under the law of Z, enforced in W." A worked example, hypothetical. A land letter of intent says the price is 5,000,000, the buyer has 60 days of exclusivity, and "neither party is bound until a definitive agreement is signed, except for the confidentiality and exclusivity clauses." The sentence reads: this binds us to confidentiality and 60 days of exclusivity, from signature, under the stated governing law, in the stated forum. It does not bind the price. If you cannot write that sentence for a document, you do not yet know what you are signing.

Question two: who pays when it goes wrong?

The hardest idea from week 21 is that the corporate wall is real, narrow at the edges, and mostly breached from the inside. Courts set aside a company's separate personality rarely, in cases of sham, fraud or domination used to cause harm. The far more common routes to personal liability are the ones you open yourself: a guarantee, a contract in your own name, a personal wrong, mixed bank accounts, or a statute that makes directors liable for particular obligations.

The applied test is a liability map: for each project, which entity signs each contract, which insurance answers which risk and to what limit, and which personal guarantees exist, with their caps and end dates. And for every change to a load path or life-safety system, a named, licensed professional who has accepted responsibility in writing, because the Hyatt Regency collapse showed that shared responsibility is nobody's.

Say that out loud now.

Question three: who taxes the result?

The hardest ideas from weeks 22 to 24 are three facts that labels cannot change. Residence follows where decisions are really made, not where an entity is registered. The character of a profit, income or capital, follows the facts of intention, holding period, financing and activity. And a tax plan that defeats the purpose of the rules it relies on can be undone by anti-avoidance rules, however carefully it obeys their words.

A second worked example, hypothetical. A developer forms a holding company abroad, intends to sell the finished building within a year, and plans to treat the gain as capital. Three facts sink all three assumptions: the decisions are made at home, so residence is in doubt; a sale within a year of completion by a developer points to income, not capital; and if the holding company has no purpose except tax, an anti-avoidance rule may disregard the benefit. The applied test is the tax map from week 23, written before any price is quoted: who pays which tax, on what amount and when, under each plausible characterisation.

Question four: who is advising whom?

The hardest idea from week 25 is that advice is only as good as its instructions, its scope and its independence. An adviser owes duties to the client named in the engagement letter, not to everyone in the room. Advice covers the facts it was given and the questions it was asked. And an adviser whose fee depends on agreeing with you, or on the size of a saving, is not independent, whatever their competence.

The applied test is three questions to put to any adviser before relying on them: whose adviser are you, what exactly did you look at, and what facts would change your view? The last question is the one that shows you the assumptions an opinion rests on.

How the best do it

Well-run institutional developers do not leave these questions to chance or to the deal team's enthusiasm. A common practice is a formal legal and tax gate before an investment committee will approve a commitment: a short memo from in-house or external counsel stating what the key documents bind the company to, a tax memo stating the expected treatment and the main risks, a list of guarantees and insurance, and confirmation of which advisers were engaged and on what scope. The committee reads those memos alongside the financial model, not after it. The memos are short, because their job is to make the decision-makers ask questions, not to replace the opinions behind them.

A small developer can copy this with a single page. Before any material signature, write the four answers yourself, attach the advisers' engagement letters, and ask one trusted person who is not on the deal to read it and ask you the hardest question they can think of. If you cannot answer it calmly, wait.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk at the end of this phase is believing that knowing the concepts replaces the professionals. It does the opposite: it makes you a demanding client, which is what good professionals want. The control is a one-page pre-signing sheet answering the four questions for every material document. Professional sign-off required: a lawyer licensed where the contract will be enforced, and a qualified tax adviser in each relevant country.

The beginner's mistake

Answering the four questions in the wrong order. A beginner starts with tax because the numbers are exciting. Start with what binds, because the contract decides who pays and who owns, and only then can tax be answered on real facts.

Callback

In week 2 you learned the pre-mortem: imagine the decision has failed and ask why. The four questions are a pre-mortem for law and tax. Imagine the deal has gone wrong five years from now and ask which document bound you, whose pocket paid, which authority taxed the result, and which adviser had not been asked the right question.

Recap

What binds, who pays, who taxes, who advises. Words and conduct bind; the corporate wall is breached mostly from inside; residence, character and purpose follow facts; and advice follows instructions. Write the four answers on one page before every signature.

Next: Ford, with Cole, Failure Forensics on a composite case: the project that spent money before it existed.
checklist: Write one sentence for each document: what it binds, from when, under which law, in which forum
Check that every letter of intent says which clauses bind and which do not
Keep a liability map for each project: signing entity, insurance, guarantees
Confirm where each entity's real decisions are made and recorded
Write the tax map before any price is quoted, under each plausible characterisation
Ask each adviser whose adviser they are, what they looked at and what would change their view
Answer the four questions on one page before every material signature
head: Field checklist
speak: Law and tax reduce to four questions you answer before every signature. First, what binds? Words and conduct do, so write one sentence for each document: it binds us to this, from this moment, under this law, in this forum. Second, who pays when it goes wrong? The corporate wall is real and courts rarely pierce it, but you breach it yourself with guarantees, contracts in your own name, mixed accounts and personal wrongs, so keep a liability map. Third, who taxes the result? Residence follows where decisions are made, character follows the facts, and a plan that defeats a rule's purpose can be undone, so write the tax map before quoting a price. Fourth, who is advising whom? Ask every adviser whose adviser they are, what they looked at and what would change their view. Answer the four in that order, on one page.
terms: Pre-signing sheet — a one-page record answering what binds, who pays, who taxes and who advises for a document
Forum — the court or tribunal that will hear disputes under a contract
Scope of engagement — the questions an adviser has been asked to answer, which limits what their advice covers

hostile.q: You've read seven weeks of law and tax. Why should I trust your judgement over your lawyer's?
hostile.a: You shouldn't, on the law. What I bring is the questions. Before I sign, I can tell you what each document binds us to, which entity and policy pays if it goes wrong, how the result is taxed under each plausible reading, and exactly what each adviser was asked and relied on. When those answers have gaps, I take them to the lawyer and the tax adviser in writing. That's what lets their judgement actually protect us.

title: The project that spent money before it existed
summary: A composite case: two partners spend months and a large sum pursuing a site before forming a company, signing contracts personally and paying from personal accounts with no agreement between them. When the deal sours, every lesson of the law and tax phase fails at once: what bound, who pays, who taxes and who was advising whom.
rule: Rule 26: No money is spent and no contract is signed for a project until the entity that will own it exists, or a written pre-formation agreement records who is paying, on whose behalf, and how it will be credited.
body:
Mr Shabazz, the most common legal and tax failure in small development is not a clever scheme gone wrong. It is ordinary spending, done early, by enthusiastic people, before there is a company or an agreement to hold it. This case is a composite, and every element of it happens.

Recall

Q. What are the four questions you answer before any material signature?

A. What binds, who pays when it goes wrong, who taxes the result, and who is advising whom, answered in that order on one page.

Q. In Deans Knight, what made the design an abuse of the loss-restriction rule?

A. It gave an outside investor the practical benefits of control and brought in a new business while staying just short of a legal acquisition of control, so it achieved what the rule exists to prevent.

Q. What is net operating income?

A. Income from a property after operating expenses and before debt service, income tax and capital spending.

Why this matters

Every project begins before its company does. You study a site, hire a consultant, pay a deposit, and talk to a partner long before anyone files incorporation papers. That gap is where law and tax are most fragile, because nobody is thinking about them yet. Cole assists today because the outcome of a case like this is decided almost entirely by what was, and was not, written down. This is a composite example; it is not any real dispute, and the legal and tax consequences in any real case depend on the law of the place and the facts, so verify them with counsel.

Step 1: Timeline

Month 1: two friends, a builder and an investor, agree over dinner to pursue a site together, "fifty-fifty." Months 2 to 7: the builder pays for a survey, a geotechnical desk study, an architect's concept and planning advice, a total of a hypothetical 180,000, from his personal account. The investor pays a 100,000 deposit to the landowner from his own company. The architect's appointment is signed by the builder in his own name. Month 8: they form a company to buy the land. Nothing is assigned to it. Month 10: land value rises sharply after a nearby rezoning, and the investor proposes bringing in a third partner with a larger share. Month 11: the builder says his 180,000 and his time make him more than an equal partner. Month 13: the deal stalls, the architect sues the builder personally for unpaid fees, and both partners dispute who owns the concept design.

Step 2: Key decisions

Three decisions created the failure: spending before an entity existed without any written record of on whose behalf the money was spent; signing a consultant's contract personally; and forming the company without assigning the earlier contracts, work and deposit to it or recording how each partner's spending would be credited.

Step 3: Assumptions

Both partners assumed that "fifty-fifty" was an agreement. It was a feeling. They assumed the company, once formed, would simply inherit everything done on its behalf. In many systems a company cannot be bound by a contract made before it existed unless it adopts or ratifies it in a way the law recognises, and the person who signed may remain personally liable. And they assumed early spending would be treated as project cost for tax, when spending by a person on behalf of an entity that did not yet exist may be hard to deduct or capitalise in the entity without proper records. Verify how the governing law treats each of these.

Step 4: Incentives

While land values were flat, neither partner had a reason to formalise anything. When the rezoning lifted values, the incentives diverged sharply: the investor wanted to dilute, the builder wanted credit for his early risk, and the absence of paper meant each could tell a plausible story. A handshake holds until the stakes change, which is exactly when you need it to hold.

Say that out loud now.

Step 5: Warning signs ignored

Invoices addressed to a person rather than a company. A consultant appointment with a personal signature block. A deposit paid from one partner's company with no note of who it was for. Spending that grew month by month with no running ledger shared between partners. A company formed with no shareholder agreement. Each one is visible, ordinary and easy to fix in the month it appears.

Step 6: Point of no return

The point of no return was the rezoning. Before it, a pre-formation agreement would have been an easy conversation between friends. After it, every term was worth real money to one side and cost real money to the other, and agreement became a negotiation, then a dispute.

Step 7: Root cause

Spending and committing before the vehicle and the agreement existed, so that the four questions of the phase had no answers: nothing defined what bound the partners to each other, the builder was personally exposed to the architect, the tax treatment of 180,000 of spending was uncertain, and no adviser had been engaged by the venture, so each partner's adviser was advising only him.

What would have changed the outcome

A two-page pre-formation agreement in month 1. It would have said: we intend to form a company to pursue this site; each of us will record the costs we pay on its behalf in a shared ledger; on formation, the company will adopt the listed contracts and reimburse or credit those costs as capital or loans at stated terms; ownership will be in stated proportions; and if we do not proceed, each bears his own costs or costs are shared in stated shares. A third page could have dealt with intellectual property in the design. Total cost: an hour with a lawyer.

Cole's evidence check

Cole's point: in a dispute like this, the court and the tax authority will both look for contemporaneous records of intention. A hypothetical example of what would have helped: an email in month 2 from the builder to the investor saying "I've paid the surveyor 12,000 on behalf of our venture company, to be credited to my capital on formation," acknowledged by the investor the same day. A dozen such emails, plus a running ledger, would have answered most of the questions that later cost both men a year and their friendship.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is early enthusiasm with no paper, because every early dollar is spent at the moment when formalising it is cheapest and feels least necessary. The control is Rule 26 and a standard pre-formation agreement you keep ready to adapt. Professional sign-off required: a corporate lawyer where the company will be formed, and a tax adviser on how pre-formation costs will be treated.

The beginner's mistake

Waiting until the deal is real to paper it. By the time a deal is real, the spending is done and the value has moved.

Rule 26

Rule 26: No money is spent and no contract is signed for a project until the entity that will own it exists, or a written pre-formation agreement records who is paying, on whose behalf, and how it will be credited.

Callback

In week 21 you met the pre-incorporation contract in the Red Pen drill: a building contract signed personally because the company was not yet registered. This case shows the same mistake repeated for months. And in week 20, a letter of intent bound what it said it bound. "Fifty-fifty" said over dinner bound nothing that either partner could later prove.

Recap

Two partners spent before forming a company, signed personally, kept no shared ledger and formed the company without assigning anything to it. When value rose, the incentives split and nothing on paper could settle it. One hour and two pages in month 1 would have prevented a year of dispute. Rule 26 is the prevention.

Next: Sage, The Money, tracing one hypothetical deal's return through every legal and tax leak of this phase.
checklist: Sign a pre-formation agreement before any shared spending on a new project
Keep a running ledger of costs each partner pays on the venture's behalf
Address every early invoice and contract to the venture, or record on whose behalf it was signed
On formation, have the company adopt the listed contracts and record how each cost is credited
Agree ownership proportions, and what happens if the project does not proceed, in writing
Deal with ownership of design work and reports in the agreement
Ask a tax adviser how pre-formation costs will be treated before you spend them
head: Field checklist
speak: This composite case is the most common legal and tax failure in small development. Two friends agree to pursue a site fifty-fifty over dinner. For months, one pays consultants from his personal account and signs the architect's contract in his own name, and the other pays the land deposit from his own company. They form a company, but assign nothing to it and record nothing about who paid what. Then a nearby rezoning lifts the land value, the incentives split, and nothing on paper can settle who owns what. The architect sues the builder personally, the early costs have an uncertain tax treatment, and each partner's adviser is advising only him. Every question of the phase fails at once: what binds, who pays, who taxes and who advises. Two pages in the first month would have prevented it. Rule 26: no spending or contract until the entity exists, or a pre-formation agreement records who pays, for whom, and how it is credited.
terms: Pre-formation agreement — a written agreement among future owners covering costs and commitments made before their company exists
Adoption of a contract — a company's act, after formation, of taking on a contract made on its behalf before it existed
Capital credit — recording a partner's contribution as equity in the venture, at an agreed value

hostile.q: You spent 180,000 before the company existed. Why should the new investor's money reimburse you?
hostile.a: Because the pre-formation agreement, signed by both founding partners in month one, lists every cost, the date and the purpose, and says each is credited to my capital at cost on formation. The company adopted the listed contracts by resolution, and the survey, geotechnical study and concept design are now its property. The ledger is in the data room. If any item isn't documented that way, I don't expect it to be credited.

title: From headline profit to money kept: the legal and tax leaks
summary: A hypothetical project's headline profit of 6,000,000 is traced through every leak this phase taught: advisers, liability costs, unrecoverable indirect tax and income tax under two characterisations. The equity multiple falls from 1.75 to between 1.38 and 1.51, and the range itself is the lesson.
body:
Mr Shabazz, a pro forma that stops at pre-tax profit is telling you what the project earns, not what you keep. Between the two sit the costs of law, liability and tax, and on a typical deal they can take a third or more of the headline. Today we follow one hypothetical project from the first number to the last.

Recall

Q. What was the root cause in the composite case of the project that spent money before it existed?

A. Spending and committing before the vehicle and an agreement existed, so nothing recorded what bound the partners, who was liable, how the costs would be taxed or who was advising the venture. Rule 26 is the prevention.

Q. Why is the expected value of an aggressive tax plan usually too high?

A. Because it ignores timing, financing reserves during a dispute, investor trust and the time a dispute consumes, and because the loss arrives late and in one lump.

Q. How do you calculate the equity multiple?

A. Total cash returned to equity divided by total equity invested. It ignores timing, which is why it is read alongside the internal rate of return.

Why this matters

Investors compare sponsors on what reaches them, and lenders on whether cash will be there when it is needed. If your model shows a strong pre-tax profit and silently assumes the friendliest legal and tax outcome, a sophisticated reader will mark it down, and an unsophisticated one may be misled. For your own wealth, the after-tax, after-leakage figure is the only one that can be spent or reinvested. All figures here are hypothetical and round, and every rate is illustrative; verify any real rate against the primary source and with a qualified adviser before relying on it.

The project

A hypothetical build-to-sell residential project. Equity of 8,000,000. Total development cost of 24,000,000, including land, hard, soft and finance costs. Total sales of 30,000,000. Headline pre-tax profit: 30,000,000 minus 24,000,000, which is 6,000,000. Headline equity multiple: equity returned of 8,000,000 plus profit of 6,000,000, divided by 8,000,000, which is 1.75.

Leak 1: the cost of law and advice

Week 25 taught that good advice is scoped, instructed and paid for. Suppose the original budget carried 100,000 for legal and tax advice, and an honest budget, covering the land contract, the entity, the construction contract, the sales documents, the tax map and a tax opinion, is 400,000. The extra 300,000 is a leak only in the sense that the model left it out. Profit falls to 5,700,000.

Leak 2: the cost of liability

Week 21 priced liability as premium, retained losses and the expected tail. Suppose the model carried insurance but no reserve for deductibles and nothing for the uninsured tail, and that honest figures add 300,000. Profit falls to 5,400,000. If you had also given a payment guarantee and paid a higher margin to cap it, as in the guarantee example, add another 60,000 of interest: profit 5,340,000.

Leak 3: indirect tax you cannot recover

Week 23 showed that value-added or goods and services tax on inputs can sometimes be recovered and sometimes not, depending on whether the sales are taxable supplies under the rules of that place. Suppose, hypothetically, that the treatment of these residential sales leaves 240,000 of input tax unrecoverable, and that the original model assumed full recovery. Profit falls to 5,100,000. Transfer tax on the land purchase was already in land cost; the question to ask is whether it was in the model at the right amount, and whether anything about the structure changes who pays it on the sale.

Say that out loud now.

Leak 4: income tax, under two characters

Week 22 showed that character follows the facts. For a developer building to sell, the honest base case is business income, with capital treatment as the optimistic alternative. Use hypothetical rates: 40 percent on business income, 20 percent on a capital gain.

As business income: tax is 40 percent of 5,100,000, which is 2,040,000. After-tax profit 3,060,000. Equity multiple: 8,000,000 plus 3,060,000, divided by 8,000,000, which is about 1.38.

As a capital gain: tax is 20 percent of 5,100,000, which is 1,020,000. After-tax profit 4,080,000. Equity multiple: 8,000,000 plus 4,080,000, divided by 8,000,000, which is 1.51.

Both multiples assume one level of tax. If the vehicle is a company and the profit must then be paid out to shareholders, a second level may apply; if it is a flow-through vehicle, the owners pay at their own rates. That is question three from Day 1, and it moves the number again.

The whole chain

StepProfitEquity multiple
Headline, pre-tax6,000,0001.75
After honest advice budget5,700,0001.71
After liability costs and guarantee margin5,340,0001.67
After unrecoverable indirect tax5,100,0001.64
After tax, as capital4,080,0001.51
After tax, as business income3,060,0001.38

From 6,000,000 to between 3,060,000 and 4,080,000. The headline overstated the kept profit by between half and nearly double. And note which leaks were in your control: the first three came from an incomplete model, not from bad luck.

Read the table aloud once and notice how it sounds to an investor. Each line is a small, explainable step, and none of them is alarming on its own. That is exactly why they get left out: each one feels too small to matter. Added together they are the difference between a deal that pays its investors well and one that merely returns their money with modest interest. A sponsor who shows this table unprompted is telling the room that the surprises have already been looked for.

A second example: what an aggressive plan does to the chain

Suppose a promoter offers a structure that would make the whole 5,100,000 taxable as capital, for a fee of 200,000, with an independent adviser's estimate of a 40 percent chance of failure, in which case the income treatment applies plus a hypothetical 300,000 of interest and penalty and 150,000 of defence costs. If it succeeds, after-tax profit is 4,080,000 minus the 200,000 fee, which is 3,880,000. If it fails, it is 3,060,000 minus 200,000, minus 300,000, minus 150,000, which is 2,410,000. Expected profit: 60 percent of 3,880,000 plus 40 percent of 2,410,000, which is 2,328,000 plus 964,000, or 3,292,000. That is 232,000 above the honest income case, and the outcomes now range from 2,410,000 to 3,880,000, with the worst arriving years late. Week 24 asked whether that trade is worth your name.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick's note for the personal balance sheet. Record project profits on your own net worth statement at the conservative character, not the hoped-for one, until the facts and the reassessment period settle it, and record any guarantee given to the project as a contingent liability beneath the line. A licensed adviser is required before you act on any personal financial decision.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is presenting the headline multiple as the investor's return. The control is a leakage table in every pro forma, from pre-tax profit to after-tax cash, with the conservative tax character as the base case and every rate labelled provisional. Professional sign-off required: a qualified tax adviser on character and rates, and an accountant on the indirect tax recovery assumption.

The beginner's mistake

Choosing the friendlier tax character as the base case because the deal looks better that way. The base case should be what the facts most likely support. The friendlier case is an upside.

Callback

In week 15 you met after-tax leakage as the gap between levered return and what an owner keeps. This lesson filled that gap with the specific leaks of the law and tax phase. And in week 13, the pro forma's soft costs included legal and insurance lines. Today showed why a token number in those lines is not a small error.

Recap

Headline 6,000,000 and 1.75. Honest advice, liability and indirect tax take it to 5,100,000. Tax at the honest income character leaves 3,060,000 and 1.38; capital would leave 4,080,000 and 1.51. Base case on the likely facts, upside on the friendly ones, and a leakage table in every model.

Next: Devika, The Rules, revisiting the rules that bite at closing.
checklist: Add a leakage table to every pro forma, from pre-tax profit to after-tax cash
Budget legal and tax advice at an honest figure, by document
Carry liability costs as premium, retained losses and expected tail
Test whether input indirect tax is recoverable on the actual sales
Use the character the facts most likely support as the base case
Show the second level of tax, or the owners' own tax, for the chosen vehicle
Label every rate provisional until an adviser has confirmed it
head: Field checklist
speak: A pre-tax profit is what a project earns, not what you keep. Take a hypothetical build-to-sell project with 8,000,000 of equity and a 6,000,000 headline profit, an equity multiple of 1.75. An honest legal and tax budget takes out 300,000. Honest liability costs and a guarantee margin take out 360,000. Unrecoverable input indirect tax takes out 240,000. That leaves 5,100,000. Taxed as business income at a hypothetical 40 percent, you keep 3,060,000, a multiple of about 1.38. Taxed as capital at 20 percent, you keep 4,080,000, or 1.51. For a developer building to sell, income is the honest base case and capital is the upside. Three of those leaks came from an incomplete model, not bad luck. So every pro forma carries a leakage table from pre-tax profit to after-tax cash, with every rate labelled provisional.
terms: Leakage table — a schedule in a pro forma tracing profit from the headline figure to after-tax cash, step by step
Input tax recovery — the ability of a business to reclaim value-added or goods and services tax paid on its costs
Base case — the scenario built on the assumptions the facts most likely support

hostile.q: Your model shows a 1.75 multiple. What will I actually receive after tax?
hostile.a: On our base case, about 1.38 times. The 1.75 is before advice, liability costs, unrecoverable indirect tax and income tax. We've assumed the profit is business income, because we are building to sell, at a provisional rate our adviser is confirming. If the facts support capital treatment, the multiple is about 1.51, but we haven't priced the deal on that. The leakage table is on page four.

title: The rules that bite at closing
summary: Most of the law and tax phase converges on a single day: closing. This lesson revisits the transaction rules that decide what that day costs: who pays transfer tax and on what, whether indirect tax applies to the sale, how the price is allocated, recapture, the seller's residence, and the contract terms that put each of those on the right side of the table.
body:
Mr Shabazz, closing is the day law and tax stop being concepts and become a cheque. Every rule this phase taught shows up on the closing statement, and a rule you did not deal with in the contract will be dealt with on that day, usually at your cost.

Recall

Q. In the leakage table, why was business income the base case for a build-to-sell project?

A. Because character follows the facts, and building to sell points to business income. Capital treatment is an upside to be shown, not assumed.

Q. What did Canada Trustco establish about the general anti-avoidance rule?

A. A three-question framework: is there a tax benefit, was the transaction undertaken mainly for it, and does it misuse or abuse the purpose of the provisions relied on. Only the third question separates acceptable planning from abuse.

Q. What is a capitalisation rate?

A. Net operating income divided by value or price. It expresses the yield a buyer accepts, and a higher rate means a lower value for the same income.

Why this matters

Transaction taxes are usually computed on the gross price, not the profit, which makes them large relative to a developer's margin, and some of them, unlike income tax, cannot be reduced by losses. They are also fixed at closing: once the transfer is registered, the amount and who paid it are settled facts. The time to manage them is when the letter of intent and the purchase agreement are drafted. Rules differ greatly between places and change often, so this is a map of the questions; verify every rate, exemption and procedure against the primary source and with a qualified adviser before relying on it.

Transfer tax: who, on what, and when

In plain English, a land transfer tax is a charge for registering a change of ownership. The questions that matter are always the same: who is legally liable for it, which amount it is charged on, whether any exemption or relief applies, and when it must be paid, usually at or shortly after registration.

The professional framing adds two refinements. First, the legal liability and the commercial cost can be different: the law may make the buyer liable, but the contract can shift the economic burden, and the price should reflect who bears it. Second, many places treat a transfer of shares in a company that mainly holds land as a transfer of the land itself. If you plan to buy or sell a company rather than the land, check first whether a land-rich company rule applies, because if it does, the share route may not save the tax, and the purchaser inherits the company's history as well.

Put a size on it, hypothetically. At an illustrative 3 percent, transfer tax on a 10,000,000 land purchase is 300,000. If the developer's target profit on the whole project is 1,500,000, that single closing line is a fifth of the margin, and it is paid before a single unit is built. A charge that size belongs in the land offer, not in the soft cost contingency.

Indirect tax on the sale

Value-added and goods and services taxes treat real estate in different ways in different places. A common pattern is that the first sale of a newly built residential property is a taxable supply, meaning a sale on which the tax is charged and which allows the seller to recover tax paid on inputs, while later resales of used residential property are often exempt, with no tax charged and no input recovery. Commercial property may be taxable, exempt or optionally taxable depending on the rules. The consequences for a developer are large: whether the sale price includes or excludes the tax, whether the seller must register and remit, and whether input tax across the whole build can be recovered.

A worked example, hypothetical. A developer sells a new building for 20,000,000. If the sale is taxable at a hypothetical 10 percent, the buyer owes 2,000,000 of tax on top of the price, unless the contract says the price is tax-inclusive. If the contract is silent and the law treats the price as tax-inclusive, the developer's net price is 20,000,000 divided by 1.10, about 18,180,000, and the developer has lost about 1,820,000 to a drafting gap. The clause that prevents it is one sentence: "The price is exclusive of any value-added or goods and services tax, which the buyer shall pay in addition."

Say that out loud now.

Allocation, recapture and character

When a property is sold, the price is often split between land, building and sometimes equipment or fixtures. The split matters because depreciation is generally allowed on buildings and equipment but not on land, so recapture, the clawing back of depreciation previously deducted, depends on how much of the price is allocated to the depreciable parts. A seller generally prefers more to land; a buyer who will hold and depreciate generally prefers more to the building. Transfer tax and indirect tax may also apply differently to different components.

A second worked example, hypothetical. A rental property bought for 10,000,000, of which 7,000,000 was building, has been depreciated so that the building's tax value is now 5,000,000. It sells for 14,000,000. If the contract allocates 8,000,000 to the building, the seller has 2,000,000 of recapture, back to the original 7,000,000 cost, and 1,000,000 of gain on the building above cost, plus the gain on land. If it allocates 6,000,000 to the building, recapture is only 1,000,000. The difference of 1,000,000 of recapture can be taxed differently from a capital gain. Authorities may challenge an allocation that does not reflect value, so it should be supported by an appraisal and agreed in the contract.

The seller's residence

Week 22 showed that land is taxed at source. Many systems therefore require a buyer purchasing from a non-resident seller to withhold part of the price, or to obtain a clearance from the authority, because the seller may otherwise leave without paying the tax on the gain. A buyer who fails to withhold where required can become liable for the tax. The control is a contract representation about the seller's residence, backed by evidence, and a mechanism for any required withholding or tax clearance, meaning a confirmation from the authority that the relevant tax has been paid or secured.

The closing tax schedule

Before you sign the purchase agreement, prepare a one-page schedule: each tax that could apply at closing, who is liable in law, who bears it under the contract, the amount it is charged on, the hypothetical amount at the expected price, the timing, and the clause that deals with it. Week 23 called this the tax map. At closing, it becomes the checklist your lawyer works from.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a purchase agreement that is silent on a transaction tax, because silence lets the law's default decide who pays, and the default is often against you. The control is the closing tax schedule, attached to the draft agreement and reviewed clause by clause. Professional sign-off required: a real estate lawyer where the land sits and a qualified indirect tax adviser.

The beginner's mistake

Negotiating the price and leaving tax to "the lawyers at closing." By closing, the price is fixed and the only question left is who absorbs the tax you forgot. Tax terms are price terms.

Callback

In week 20, conditions precedent decided when obligations started. At closing, tax clearances and withholding mechanisms are often written as conditions, and they deserve the same care. And in week 23, Rule 23 said no price is quoted until the tax map is written. Today the tax map became clauses.

Recap

Transfer tax: who pays, on what, when, and whether share routes are caught. Indirect tax: taxable or exempt, inclusive or exclusive, and input recovery. Allocation drives recapture. A non-resident seller may trigger withholding. Put each in the contract before the price is final.

Next: Nadia, The Numbers, working backward from a seller's after-tax target to the price that delivers it.
checklist: Prepare a closing tax schedule before signing any purchase agreement
State in the contract whether the price includes or excludes indirect tax
Check whether a land-rich company rule catches any share transfer
Agree the allocation of price between land, building and equipment, supported by an appraisal
Model recapture on the agreed allocation before accepting it
Confirm the seller's residence and any withholding or clearance requirement
Have the lawyer work from the schedule clause by clause at closing
head: Field checklist
speak: Closing is where law and tax become a cheque, so deal with every transaction tax in the contract before the price is final. For transfer tax, ask who is liable, on what amount, with which exemptions, and when, and check whether selling shares in a land-rich company is treated as selling the land. For value-added or goods and services tax, ask whether the sale is taxable or exempt, and say in the contract whether the price includes or excludes it; silence on a hypothetical 20,000,000 sale can cost about 1,820,000. Agree how the price is split between land, building and equipment, because that split drives recapture of past depreciation. And if the seller is non-resident, the buyer may have to withhold or obtain a clearance. Put it all on a one-page closing tax schedule and attach it to the draft agreement.
terms: Taxable supply — a sale on which value-added or goods and services tax is charged and which allows recovery of input tax
Purchase price allocation — the agreed split of a property's price between land, building and other components
Tax clearance — a confirmation from a tax authority that the tax on a transaction has been paid or secured

hostile.q: The contract doesn't say whether the price includes sales tax. Why is that my problem rather than the seller's?
hostile.a: It may be both our problem, depending on the default rule, and I don't want a court deciding it. I've proposed a clause stating the price is exclusive of value-added tax, with the buyer paying it in addition, and we've checked whether this sale is a taxable supply at all. Until that clause is agreed, I treat the price as uncertain by the full amount of the tax.

title: Working backward from what the seller wants to keep
summary: Starting from a finished outcome, a hypothetical seller who wants 5,000,000 of cash after tax and debt, this lesson works backward through selling costs, recapture and capital gains to the price of 12,500,000 that delivers it. A second reverse problem finds the most a buyer can pay, and shows the gap between the two.
body:
Mr Shabazz, a seller does not really want a price. He wants an amount of cash in his account after the loan, the costs and the tax. If you can work backward from that amount to a price, you know his real number, and you know which levers close a gap that the headline price cannot.

Recall

Q. How does the allocation of a sale price between land and building affect the seller?

A. Depreciation is generally allowed on buildings but not land, so more price allocated to the building generally means more recapture of past depreciation, which may be taxed differently from a capital gain.

Q. A notice totals 1.68 times the tax. How do you find the disallowed deduction?

A. Divide the notice by 1.68 to get the tax, then divide the tax by the rate. At a hypothetical 25 percent, a 1,680,000 notice means 1,000,000 of tax and 4,000,000 of deductions.

Q. How do you value a property from its net operating income?

A. Divide the net operating income by the capitalisation rate. On 900,000 of income at 7 percent, value is about 12,860,000.

Why this matters

Negotiations stall on price when each side is really arguing about something else: a seller's tax bill, a buyer's closing costs, a lender's payoff. Working backward from what each side needs to keep shows you where the real gap is, and often reveals that it can be closed by allocation, timing or who pays which cost rather than by moving the price. On even-numbered weeks we reverse engineer. Every rate here is hypothetical and simplified; the seller's real tax is a matter for his own adviser, and you should never advise him on it.

The outcome: 5,000,000 kept

A hypothetical seller owns a rental building. He wants 5,000,000 of cash after repaying his loan and paying his tax. The facts: original cost 10,000,000, of which 3,000,000 was land and 7,000,000 building; the building's remaining tax value, its cost less depreciation claimed, is 5,000,000; the loan to repay is 6,000,000; selling costs are 2 percent of the price; the resale is assumed exempt from indirect tax; and the buyer bears the transfer tax. Hypothetical rates: recapture taxed at 40 percent; gain above original cost taxed at 20 percent. The building is allocated at its original cost of 7,000,000, so recapture is the full depreciation claimed.

Step 1: the recapture

Recapture is the original building cost minus its tax value: 7,000,000 minus 5,000,000, which is 2,000,000. Tax on it, at 40 percent, is 800,000. This part does not depend on the price, as long as the building is allocated at least its original cost.

Step 2: express the gain in terms of the price

Call the price P. Net proceeds after selling costs are 0.98 P. The gain above original cost is 0.98 P minus 10,000,000. Tax on it, at 20 percent, is 0.196 P minus 2,000,000.

Step 3: write the seller's cash in terms of P

Cash kept equals net proceeds, minus the loan, minus both taxes. That is 0.98 P, minus 6,000,000, minus 800,000, minus (0.196 P minus 2,000,000). Collect the terms in P: 0.98 P minus 0.196 P is 0.784 P. Collect the fixed amounts: minus 6,000,000, minus 800,000, plus 2,000,000, which is minus 4,800,000. So cash kept equals 0.784 P minus 4,800,000.

Step 4: solve

Set 0.784 P minus 4,800,000 equal to 5,000,000. Then 0.784 P equals 9,800,000, and P equals 9,800,000 divided by 0.784, which is 12,500,000.

Tie-out, forward: selling costs 250,000, net proceeds 12,250,000. Gain above cost 2,250,000, tax 450,000. Recapture tax 800,000. Total tax 1,250,000. Loan 6,000,000. Cash kept: 12,250,000 minus 6,000,000 minus 1,250,000, which is 5,000,000. The seller's real number is a price of 12,500,000.

What the formula tells you about him

The figure 0.784 is worth reading on its own. It says that for every extra dollar of price, the seller keeps about 78 cents after selling costs and gain tax. Turn it around: for him to keep an extra 100,000, the price must rise by 100,000 divided by 0.784, about 127,600. That is why a seller who says he needs "another hundred thousand" is really asking for more than that, and why a concession that reduces his tax can be worth more to him than an equal concession on price. The formula is a map of his incentives.

Say that out loud now.

A second reverse problem: the buyer's ceiling

Now work backward from the buyer. The building earns net operating income of 900,000. The buyer requires a 7 percent yield on everything it spends to acquire it, not just the price. It bears transfer tax at a hypothetical 3 percent of the price and other closing costs of 1 percent.

Step 1: the most the buyer can spend in total is 900,000 divided by 0.07, which is about 12,857,000.

Step 2: total spend is the price times 1.04, because transfer tax and closing costs add 4 percent. So the maximum price is 12,857,000 divided by 1.04, which is about 12,363,000. Note the method: divide by one plus the cost rate. Do not subtract 4 percent of 12,857,000, which gives a slightly different and wrong answer.

The gap, and what closes it

The seller needs 12,500,000. The buyer can pay about 12,363,000. The gap is about 137,000. A beginner would split the difference on price and both sides would walk away unhappy. A professional asks which non-price terms move either side's number.

Here are two, hypothetical. First, allocation: if the facts support allocating more of the price to land and less to the building, below its original cost, part of the seller's recapture may fall away, and some of it may become capital gain taxed at the lower rate, which lowers the price the seller needs. But the buyer then has less to depreciate, which matters to a buyer who will hold, and any allocation must reflect real value, supported by an appraisal, or it invites challenge. Second, cost sharing: if the seller pays half of the buyer's 1 percent closing costs, about 62,000, the buyer's ceiling rises by roughly that amount, while the seller's net falls by somewhat less once his own tax deduction for the cost is counted, subject to his adviser's view. Neither lever alone closes 137,000, but together with a small price move, they might. The reverse calculation tells you where to look.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is negotiating the headline price without knowing either side's real number. The control is to rebuild, before any price discussion, the seller's likely cash-kept calculation and your own all-in ceiling, and to list the non-price terms that move each. Professional sign-off required: your own tax adviser on your side, and the seller's adviser on his. Never advise the other side on its tax.

The beginner's mistake

Treating transfer tax and closing costs as an afterthought to the yield. A buyer who computes its ceiling on the price alone overpays by the costs on top, which here is about 4 percent, more than the gap that the whole negotiation was about.

Callback

In week 17 you reverse engineered a land price from public information. Today you reverse engineered a seller's price from his tax position. And in week 22, Nadia said gross up by dividing by one minus the rate, never by adding the rate. The buyer's ceiling used the mirror of the same rule: divide by one plus the cost rate. The algebra of this phase is short, and it is the same each time.

Recap

A seller wanting 5,000,000 after a 6,000,000 loan, 800,000 of recapture tax and a 20 percent gain tax needs 12,500,000. A buyer needing 7 percent on 900,000 of income, with 4 percent of acquisition costs on top, can pay about 12,363,000. The 137,000 gap is a list of non-price levers, not a fight over price.

Next: Vera, The Room, a full mock closing-readiness meeting with your lawyer, tax adviser and the lender's counsel.
checklist: Rebuild the seller's likely cash-kept calculation before any price talk
Compute your own ceiling on total acquisition cost, not price alone
Divide by one plus the cost rate when backing out a maximum price
Tie out every reverse calculation forward to the target
List the non-price levers: allocation, cost sharing, timing, who pays which tax
Support any price allocation with an appraisal
Never advise the other side on its own tax; send it to its own adviser
head: Field checklist
speak: A seller wants cash kept, not a price, so work backward from it. Take a hypothetical seller who wants 5,000,000 after repaying a 6,000,000 loan. His building cost 10,000,000, with 7,000,000 of building now at a tax value of 5,000,000, so recapture is 2,000,000, taxed at a hypothetical 40 percent, or 800,000. The gain above cost, after 2 percent selling costs, is taxed at 20 percent. Writing his cash in terms of the price gives 0.784 times the price, minus 4,800,000. Set that to 5,000,000 and the price is 12,500,000. Now the buyer: 900,000 of income at a required 7 percent allows about 12,857,000 of total spend, and with 4 percent of transfer tax and closing costs on top, the ceiling price is about 12,363,000. The 137,000 gap is a list of non-price levers like allocation and cost sharing, not a fight over price.
terms: Tax value — the cost of a depreciable asset less the tax depreciation already claimed on it
Cash kept — the amount a seller retains after selling costs, debt repayment and tax
Price ceiling — the most a buyer can pay while still meeting its required return on total acquisition cost

hostile.q: The seller wants 12,500,000 and you're offering 12,363,000. Why should he move?
hostile.a: Because I'm not asking him to take less cash; I'm asking him to look at how he gets it. I've offered to share our closing costs, and if his appraiser supports a different land and building split, his adviser may find his tax falls. Our ceiling is set by the building's income and our acquisition costs, and I've shown him how. If those levers don't close it with a small price move, we'll both walk away friends.

title: Mock meeting: is this deal ready to close?
summary: A full mock closing-readiness meeting on a hypothetical land acquisition, with your lawyer, your tax adviser and the lender's counsel. You chair. The lesson scripts the agenda, the lines to say and never to say, the question behind each adviser's answer, when to stay silent, and the one conversation that must happen in a separate room.
body:
Mr Shabazz, a closing-readiness meeting is where you find out whether the four questions of this phase have real answers. You chair it, you run it from a one-page agenda, and you leave with a written list of what is ready, what is not, and who owns each gap.

Recall

Q. A seller wants 5,000,000 of cash kept and his formula is 0.784 times the price minus 4,800,000. What price does he need?

A. 12,500,000, because 9,800,000 divided by 0.784 is 12,500,000.

Q. What is the difference between tax and interest on a reassessment, and civil penalties?

A. Tax and interest follow a position that was honestly taken but failed. Civil penalties follow conduct below a standard, such as carelessness or a knowing position. Records of advice, decision and disclosure decide which applies.

Q. What is yield on cost?

A. Stabilised net operating income divided by total development cost, the return the project earns on what it cost to build.

Why this matters

Deals fail at closing for reasons everyone in the room could have spotted a month earlier: an unsigned consent, a tax clearance not applied for, a guarantee whose wording nobody read, a contract signed by the wrong entity. A disciplined readiness meeting two to three weeks before closing catches them while there is still time. It is also where you show your advisers and your lender that the owner is in control of the process, which changes how carefully they work. The scene is hypothetical; nothing in it is advice about any real transaction.

The setting

A hypothetical acquisition of a development site for 8,000,000, through a newly formed project company, funded by 3,000,000 of equity and a 5,000,000 land loan. Closing is in three weeks. In the room: your real estate lawyer, your tax adviser, and the lender's counsel. Your partner joins by phone. You chair, and you have circulated a one-page agenda two days before.

The agenda

  1. What binds: purchase agreement, conditions, consents and title.
  2. Who pays: signing entity, guarantees, insurance from closing.
  3. Who taxes: the closing tax schedule.
  4. Lender conditions precedent.
  5. The open list: item, owner, date.

Opening lines

"Thank you for coming. The purpose is to confirm, item by item, that we can close in three weeks, and to leave with a written list of anything that is not ready, who owns it and by when. I'll go through the agenda in order. Please tell me what you have not seen, not only what you have."

That last sentence matters. Advisers report on what they reviewed. You need to know what they did not review, because that is where closings fail.

Item 1: what binds

You: "Which conditions in the purchase agreement are still open, and what happens to the deposit if any of them fails?" Your lawyer lists two: a consent from the holder of an easement and the seller's delivery of a clean title.

The question behind your lawyer's answer is often "the easement holder has not replied and I don't want to alarm you." Ask: "If the consent is not in by closing, what are our options under the agreement?" Then stay silent until you have the full answer, including any deadline to extend.

Item 2: who pays

You: "Confirm the purchase agreement and the loan are both in the project company's exact legal name, that any pre-formation costs have been adopted by resolution, and that insurance is in place from the moment of closing." Then, to the lender's counsel: "Please confirm the guarantee is capped at the agreed amount and releases on the agreed milestone. I want to see the final wording of those two clauses this week."

If the lender's counsel says "it's our standard form," you say: "Understood. I'll need the cap and the release in the form we agreed in the term sheet. Can you send the marked draft by Friday?" Acknowledge, bridge, answer, as in week 6.

Say that out loud now.

Item 3: who taxes

You, to your tax adviser: "Walk us through the closing tax schedule. For each tax, who is liable, on what amount, when it is paid, and which clause deals with it. Then tell me which assumption you are least comfortable with."

The adviser says transfer tax is the buyer's at a provisional rate she is still confirming, the sale is assumed exempt from indirect tax because the land is undeveloped, which she wants to confirm, and the seller has represented that it is resident, with no evidence yet supplied. The question behind her answer is: "I'm not ready to sign off on two of these." Your line: "Thank you. Then those are two open items. What do you need, from whom, by when?"

The conversation for a separate room

Your tax adviser mentions that the seller may push to restructure the sale as a share sale. Do not discuss your tax strategy for responding to that in front of the lender's counsel. In many systems, communications with your lawyer for the purpose of legal advice can be protected by privilege, but disclosing them to a third party, such as the other side's or the lender's lawyer, can waive that protection. Say: "Let's take that offline with our own team after this meeting." Week 25 covered privilege in concept; verify how it applies in your jurisdiction with counsel.

Item 4: lender conditions

Ask the lender's counsel to read out every condition precedent not yet satisfied. Write each one down with an owner. Do not accept "we're nearly there" for any condition; ask "what document, from whom, by when?"

Item 5: the open list, and the close

Read the list aloud: easement consent, title evidence, the transfer tax rate, the indirect tax position, the seller's residence evidence, the guarantee wording and three lender conditions. Assign each an owner and a date. Then close: "I'll circulate this list by end of day. If any item is not resolved by the date beside it, I want to hear about it the day before, not on the day."

The lines never to say

  • "I'm sure it'll all come together." It tells every adviser that the owner will not chase.
  • "Just get it done, whatever it takes." It invites shortcuts, including on the documents that later decide disputes.
  • "Don't put that in writing." Records made at the time are your protection; asking for them not to exist is the start of every bad file.
  • "We'll sort the tax out after closing." As Devika said on Day 4: after closing, the only question left is who absorbs it.

Holding your state

You will hear several problems in a row, and the room will watch how you take them. Keep your voice even, write each one down, and say "thank you, that's useful" to bad news. Advisers who are thanked for bad news bring it to you early. Advisers who are blamed for it learn to bring it late.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is leaving the meeting with reassurance instead of a list. The control is a written open-items list, every item with a named owner and a date, circulated the same day and reviewed every two or three days until closing. Professional sign-off required: your real estate lawyer and your tax adviser, each confirming in writing that their items are closed.

The beginner's mistake

Asking advisers what they have done rather than what they have not seen. The first gets a progress report. The second gets the risk.

Callback

In week 25 you learned to ask every adviser what facts would change their view. In this meeting the same question, put to the tax adviser, surfaced two unready items. And in week 5, the rule of three and bottom line first shaped the opening: purpose, process, output. A meeting chaired that way ends on time with a list.

Recap

Circulate a one-page agenda built on the four questions. Ask what has not been seen. Turn every soft answer into an item, an owner and a date. Take privileged strategy into a separate room. Thank people for bad news. Leave with a written list, and chase it.

Next: Kema, the Checkpoint: a mock interview on the whole law and tax phase, a recorded explanation, and the rules you will not break.
checklist: Circulate a one-page agenda built on the four questions two days before
Ask each adviser what they have not seen, not only what they have
Turn every open point into an item with an owner and a date
Confirm every closing document is in the exact name of the right entity
Read the guarantee cap and release clauses yourself before closing
Discuss privileged strategy only with your own team, outside the meeting
Circulate the open-items list the same day and review it every few days
head: Field checklist
speak: A closing-readiness meeting, two to three weeks before closing, is where the four questions of this phase get real answers. Circulate a one-page agenda: what binds, who pays, who taxes, the lender's conditions, and the open list. Open by asking every adviser to tell you what they have not seen, not only what they have, because that is where closings fail. Ask your lawyer which conditions are open and what happens to the deposit if one fails. Confirm every document is in the project company's exact name, pre-formation costs are adopted and insurance runs from closing. Ask your tax adviser which assumption she is least comfortable with. Take any privileged strategy into a separate room, away from the lender's counsel. Turn every soft answer into an item, an owner and a date, thank people for bad news, and circulate the list the same day.
terms: Closing-readiness meeting — a meeting before closing to confirm, item by item, that every document, consent and condition is in place
Open-items list — a written list of unresolved closing matters, each with an owner and a date
Waiver of privilege — loss of the protection over confidential legal communications, for example by disclosing them to a third party

hostile.q: Lender's counsel: Our guarantee is our standard form. Why are you holding up closing over two clauses?
hostile.a: I'm not holding up closing; I'm making sure we close on what was agreed. The term sheet set a cap and a release at stabilisation, and the standard form has neither. I've sent a marked draft of just those two clauses, and if they're agreed this week, nothing else in the timetable moves.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Checkpoint: law and tax foundations
summary: The checkpoint for the law and tax phase: a six-question mock interview with model answers, a recorded three-minute explanation scored from 1 to 5 on accuracy, structure, composure and the hard question, and a reading of every rule you have committed to so far.
body:
Mr Shabazz, a phase is learned when you can explain it under pressure, out loud, in three minutes, without notes. Law and tax are the subjects where that is hardest, because the words sound simple and the ideas are not. Today you find out where you stand, and you write down the score.

Recall

Q. In a closing-readiness meeting, what question surfaces the most risk?

A. "What have you not seen?" Advisers report on what they reviewed; closings fail on what nobody reviewed.

Q. What is Rule 24?

A. No tax plan goes ahead unless I can state its commercial purpose in one sentence and would be content to hand every document to the tax authority on the first day.

Q. What does a cap rate of 7 percent imply about value on 1,000,000 of net operating income?

A. A value of about 14,290,000, which is 1,000,000 divided by 0.07.

Why this matters

In the money phase, an error shows up in a spreadsheet. In the law and tax phase, an error shows up years later, in a letter from a lawyer or an authority, when the facts can no longer be changed. That makes it the phase where recognition is most dangerous. You may recognise every term and still be unable to use it in a meeting. This checkpoint tests use, not recognition, and it gives you a score you can compare at the next one.

The mock interview

Imagine an experienced investor across the table. Read each question, answer it aloud before you read the model answer, then compare. Be strict.

Question 1. You've signed a letter of intent on land at 5,000,000. Are you bound to buy it?

Answer: Only if the letter says so or our conduct shows a concluded deal. Ours states that only the confidentiality and exclusivity clauses bind, and that nothing else binds until a definitive agreement is signed, so I am bound to keep it confidential and not to shop the site during exclusivity, and not to pay 5,000,000. I can say in one sentence what each document binds us to, from when, under which law, in which forum.

Question 2. Your project company has 2,000,000 of equity. If a claim of 10,000,000 hits it, what do you personally lose?

Answer: My equity in that company, plus anything I have opened the wall to myself: any guarantee, capped and dated on my schedule, any contract I signed personally, and any personal wrong. The insurance is the first answer to the claim, sized to the realistic worst case. Courts pierce the veil only in narrow cases like a sham or fraud, and we run each company separately so that question does not arise.

Question 3. Your holding company is incorporated abroad. Is it resident abroad for tax?

Answer: Not because of where it is incorporated. Residence follows where central management and control actually sits, as Fundy Settlement showed. So the board meets where the company is meant to be managed, with directors who have the information and authority to decide, and the minutes and emails prove it. Rule 22.

Question 4. Will the profit on this project be taxed as capital?

Answer: I don't assume it. The facts decide: intention, holding period, financing and activity. Because we are building to sell, my base case is business income, and capital is the upside. On our hypothetical numbers, that is the difference between a 1.38 and a 1.51 multiple, and I've priced the deal on 1.38.

Question 5. An adviser offers a structure that saves most of the tax. Why not use it?

Answer: I'll consider any plan that has a commercial purpose I can state in one sentence and works with every document on the table. If it relies on defeating the purpose of a rule, it is avoidance and can be undone, as in Deans Knight; if it relies on the authority not knowing the facts, it is evasion. I price uncertain plans as bets, with interest, penalties, financing reserves and investor trust included, and I take independent advice from someone not paid on the saving.

Question 6. What happened in your composite case of the project that spent money before it existed, and what did you learn?

Answer: Two partners spent and signed personally before forming a company, with no agreement, and when land values rose nothing on paper could settle who owned what or who owed the architect. Rule 26: no spending or contract until the entity exists, or a written pre-formation agreement records who pays, on whose behalf, and how it is credited.

Say that out loud now.

The recorded explanation

Now the real test. Take out your phone, open the voice recorder, and record a three-minute explanation of this phase as if to a new partner who has never dealt with lawyers or tax advisers. Use this structure: the four questions, what binds, who pays, who taxes and who advises; one idea behind each; one failure case with its rule; and the single risk you would watch most closely on your next deal. No notes. Do not restart if you stumble; stumbling is data.

Listen back once and score yourself from 1 to 5 on each of four measures:

  1. Accuracy. Were the definitions right, and did you avoid stating any law, rate or deadline as fact? A 5 has no errors; a 3 has one material slip, such as calling a partnership tax-free.
  2. Structure. Did you give the four questions in order, with the bottom line first? A 5 could be written down as an outline.
  3. Composure. Was your pace steady through the tax section, with pauses instead of filler? A 5 sounds practised.
  4. The hard question. Did you name, unprompted, where you are personally exposed and what you would refuse to do? A 5 raises the hard point before the listener can.

Write the four scores and the date in your decision journal. A worked example of honest scoring: if you explained residence correctly but said "the company is resident where it's incorporated" once in passing, accuracy is a 3, because that sentence is exactly the mistake the phase taught you not to make. If you spent the first minute describing the cases before stating the four questions, structure is a 3.

What to do with the scores

Act on your lowest score alone this week. If accuracy was lowest, reread the lesson the error came from and rewrite the idea in one sentence. If structure was lowest, write the four questions on a card and record again tomorrow from the card. If composure was lowest, record again deliberately slower and count the filler words. If the hard question was lowest, open the next recording with "Here is where I am personally exposed, and here is what I will not do." Record once more at the end of the week, compare, and keep both recordings for the next checkpoint.

Rules I will not break

Below this lesson is the list of rules you have committed to so far, one from each failure case, including Rules 19 to 26 from this phase. Read each rule below aloud, then restate it in your own words. If you cannot restate a rule without looking, mark it and reread the lesson it came from this week. The rules from this phase protect you in moments when someone is pressing you to sign today; a rule you cannot say from memory will not be there in that moment.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk at this checkpoint is grading yourself on what you meant rather than what you said. Law and tax are full of sentences that are almost right. The control is the recording: score the tape, not the intention.

The beginner's mistake

Skipping the recording and reading the model answers instead. Reading gives the feeling of mastery without the evidence. The discomfort of hearing yourself explain residence or character aloud is the training.

Callback

In week 6 you learned to answer hostile questions by acknowledging, bridging and answering, and to say "I'll confirm by Friday" rather than guess. Law and tax are where that line earns its keep: when you are asked a legal or tax question you cannot answer with confidence, "I'll confirm that with counsel by Friday" is the professional answer, and inventing one is the amateur's.

Recap

Answer the six questions aloud before reading the model answers. Record three minutes on the phase without notes, score accuracy, structure, composure and the hard question from 1 to 5, and write the scores in your journal. Then read every rule aloud and restate it.

Next: Remi opens the markets, land and approvals phase with cycles: supply, credit, interest rates, cap rates and timing.
checklist: RULES_SO_FAR
head: Rules I will not break
speak: Mr Shabazz, this is the checkpoint for law and tax. Before any signature, I answer four questions in order. What binds: words and conduct, so I can say in one sentence what each document commits us to, from when, under which law and in which forum. Who pays: the corporate wall is real and rarely pierced by courts, but I open it myself with guarantees, contracts in my own name and mixed accounts, so every project company is run separately, insured to the realistic worst claim, and every guarantee is capped and dated. Who taxes: residence follows decisions, character follows facts, and a plan that defeats a rule's purpose can be undone, so my base case is the conservative character and every rate is provisional. Who advises: I ask each adviser whose adviser they are, what they looked at and what would change their view. Now record three minutes without notes, score yourself, and read your rules aloud.
terms: Checkpoint — a scheduled test of a whole phase, done out loud and scored, so progress can be measured
Recognition — knowing a term when you see it, which is weaker than being able to use it under pressure
Decision journal — a dated record of decisions, the reasons for them and later scores, used to measure and improve judgement

hostile.q: You've spent eight weeks on law and tax. In one minute, why should I trust you not to get us into legal or tax trouble?
hostile.a: Because I won't sign until four questions have written answers: what binds us, who pays if it goes wrong, who taxes the result, and who is advising whom on what scope. My personal exposure is limited to listed, capped guarantees. Our tax base case is the conservative one, and I don't use any plan I couldn't defend with every document on the table. And when I don't know, I say I'll confirm with counsel by Friday, and I do.
